a: A slack hand at work leaves a person poor,
t: A different line and an added couplet in the Greek
p: The Greek opens "Poverty humbles a man" and adds a couplet after the verse (10:4a).

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); all Hebrew manuscripts
readings.en: poor is one who works with a slack palm
readings.plain: A slack hand at work leaves a person poor,

readings.w: Septuagint, the Old Greek of Proverbs: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed in Swete's edition (checked); Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus also have the couplet
readings.orig: πενία ἄνδρα ταπεινοῖ ... (4a) υἱὸς πεπαιδευμένος σοφὸς ἔσται, τῷ δὲ ἄφρονι διακόνῳ χρήσεται
readings.en: Poverty humbles a man ... (4a) An instructed son will be wise, and will use the fool as a servant
readings.plain: Poverty brings a man low, ... An instructed son will be wise, / and he will make the fool his servant.

why: The Hebrew line is about the slack worker; the Greek turns it into a general saying about poverty, perhaps reading the consonants differently, and adds a couplet that links 10:4 with the wise son of 10:1 and 10:5. The added couplet is found only in the Greek. The Plain follows the Hebrew.

a: and a stubborn fool who keeps talking is brought down.
t: A repeated line, or a lost contrast?
p: The Hebrew repeats 10:8b. The Greek has a contrasting line about open rebuke.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); all Hebrew manuscripts; KJV
readings.en: and a fool of lips will be thrown down
readings.plain: and a stubborn fool who keeps talking is brought down.

readings.w: Septuagint, the Old Greek of Proverbs: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed in Swete's edition (checked)
readings.orig: ὁ δὲ ἐλέγχων μετὰ παρρησίας εἰρηνοποιεῖ
readings.en: but the one who rebukes with boldness makes peace
readings.plain: but one who rebukes openly makes peace.

why: Every Hebrew manuscript repeats the second line of 10:8 here. Many scholars think the Greek keeps the original contrast (the sly winker against the open rebuker), and some modern versions follow it. But the collectors reused half-lines often (10:6b and 10:11b), so a repeat is not proof of a copying error. The Plain keeps the Hebrew and shows the Greek here.

a: treacherous people are ruined by their own twisting.
p: The marginal reading has a verb, "destroys them"; the written text has a noun, "their destruction".

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (AD 1008): the reading the Masoretes marked to be read aloud (Qere); most modern versions
readings.en: it destroys them
readings.plain: treacherous people are ruined by their own twisting.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex: the written consonants (Ketiv)
readings.en: and their destruction
readings.plain: the crookedness of the treacherous is their destruction.

why: The two forms differ only in vowels and one letter, and the meaning is the same: the treacherous are ruined by their own crookedness. The Plain follows the marginal reading, as most translations do.

a: Upright people are led by their own integrity;
t: A different verse in the Greek
p: The Greek has a different saying: a righteous man dies leaving regret, and the ungodly's ruin is quick.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); all Hebrew manuscripts
readings.en: the integrity of the upright guides them
readings.plain: Upright people are led by their own integrity;

readings.w: Septuagint, the Old Greek of Proverbs: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed in Swete's edition (checked); Sinaiticus agrees; Alexandrinus adds before it a Greek form of the Hebrew 11:3 and 11:4
readings.orig: ἀποθανὼν δίκαιος ἔλιπεν μετάμελον, πρόχειρος δὲ γίνεται καὶ ἐπίχαρτος ἀσεβῶν ἀπώλεια
readings.en: A righteous man at his death leaves regret, but the destruction of the ungodly comes quickly and gives joy
readings.plain: When a righteous man dies, he leaves people grieving, / but the ruin of the wicked comes fast and brings joy.

why: The Greek verse has little in common with the Hebrew; it may be a free rewriting or a different saying that took its place, and its second half is close to 11:10. Codex Alexandrinus shows a scribe adding a translation of the Hebrew. The Plain follows the Hebrew.

a: When a wicked person dies, his hope comes to an end,
p: This entry goes with the next. The Greek turns the verse around: when a righteous man dies, his hope does not perish.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); all Hebrew manuscripts; KJV
readings.en: at the death of a wicked man hope perishes
readings.plain: When a wicked person dies, his hope comes to an end,

readings.w: Septuagint, the Old Greek of Proverbs: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed in Swete's edition (checked)
readings.orig: τελευτήσαντος ἀνδρὸς δικαίου οὐκ ὄλλυται ἐλπίς
readings.en: when a righteous man dies, hope does not perish
readings.plain: When a righteous man dies, his hope does not come to an end,

why: The Hebrew makes both lines about the wicked. The Greek makes the verse a contrast, and in doing so speaks of a hope that outlasts death, a theme of the later Jewish wisdom of its time (compare Wisdom of Solomon 3:1–4). That looks like the translator's interpretation, so the Plain keeps the Hebrew.

a: and the hope he placed in strength has perished.
p: This entry goes with the one before. The Greek's second line is about the boast of the ungodly.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); all Hebrew manuscripts; KJV
readings.en: and the hope of strength (or of wealth) has perished
readings.plain: and the hope he placed in strength has perished.

readings.w: Septuagint, the Old Greek of Proverbs: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed in Swete's edition (checked)
readings.orig: τὸ δὲ καύχημα τῶν ἀσεβῶν ὄλλυται
readings.en: but the boast of the ungodly perishes
readings.plain: but the boast of the wicked comes to an end.

why: 'Onim can mean strength or wealth; some read it as a form of 'aven, "wicked men", which would give "the hope of the wicked". The Greek's "the ungodly" may reflect that reading. The Plain keeps the Hebrew word in its common sense.

a: and the ruthless take hold of riches.
p: The Greek turns the verse into four lines about two kinds of wives and two kinds of men.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); all Hebrew manuscripts; KJV
readings.en: and ruthless men take hold of wealth
readings.plain: and the ruthless take hold of riches.

readings.w: Septuagint, the Old Greek of Proverbs: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed in Swete's edition (checked)
readings.orig: θρόνος δὲ ἀτιμίας γυνὴ μισοῦσα δίκαια. πλούτου ὀκνηροὶ ἐνδεεῖς γίνονται, οἱ δὲ ἀνδρεῖοι ἐρείδονται πλούτῳ
readings.en: but a woman hating righteousness is a throne of dishonor; the lazy become needy of wealth, but the manly prop themselves on wealth
readings.plain: but a woman who hates what is right is a seat of dishonor. / The lazy come to lack wealth, / but the hard-working prop themselves up with wealth.

why: The Greek begins "A gracious wife raises up glory for her husband" and then adds the lines shown. Some scholars think the Hebrew lost two half-lines here, since the four-line Greek has a neat double contrast. No Hebrew manuscript has them, so the Plain keeps the Hebrew couplet.

a: and one who wins people over is wise.
p: The Hebrew says the wise "take lives". The Greek and many scholars read a contrast about violence.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); all Hebrew manuscripts; KJV
readings.en: and one who takes lives is wise
readings.plain: and one who wins people over is wise.

readings.w: Septuagint, the Old Greek of Proverbs: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed in Swete's edition (checked)
readings.en: but the lives of the lawless are taken away before their time
readings.plain: but the lives of the lawless are taken away before their time.

readings.w: Proposed correction (many commentators): חָמָס for חָכָם
readings.en: but violence takes lives
readings.plain: but violence takes lives away.

why: "Takes lives" usually means "kills", which is why scholars have suggested reading chamas, "violence", instead of chakham, "wise": the letters are close. The Greek seems to support a contrast with the first line. But the Hebrew can mean "captures people", winning them over (compare 6:25), and it is the reading of every manuscript, so the Plain keeps it. See the note.

a: if the righteous get their due here on earth,
p: This entry goes with the next. The Greek, quoted in 1 Peter 4:18, says the righteous are saved only with difficulty.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); all Hebrew manuscripts; KJV
readings.en: look, the righteous is repaid on the earth
readings.plain: if the righteous get their due here on earth,

readings.w: Septuagint, the Old Greek of Proverbs: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed in Swete's edition (checked); quoted in 1 Peter 4:18
readings.orig: εἰ ὁ μὲν δίκαιος μόλις σῴζεται
readings.en: if the righteous is barely saved
readings.plain: if the righteous is saved only with difficulty,

why: The Greek translator may have read yeshullam, "repaid", in a sense close to "made whole, saved", and supplied "barely" to keep the argument from lesser to greater. Peter's letter follows the Greek. The Plain keeps the Hebrew, and the note shows how 1 Peter uses the Greek.

a: how much more the wicked man and the sinner!
p: This entry goes with the one before. The Greek asks where the ungodly and the sinner will appear.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); all Hebrew manuscripts; KJV
readings.en: how much more the wicked and the sinner
readings.plain: how much more the wicked man and the sinner!

readings.w: Septuagint, the Old Greek of Proverbs: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed in Swete's edition (checked); quoted in 1 Peter 4:18
readings.orig: ὁ ἀσεβὴς καὶ ἁμαρτωλὸς ποῦ φανεῖται
readings.en: where will the ungodly and sinner appear?
readings.plain: where will the ungodly and the sinner show up?

why: Both forms make the same "how much more" argument. The Greek puts it as a question about the judgment, which is how 1 Peter 4:18 uses it.

a: who has a servant
t: Has a servant, or serves himself?
p: With different vowels the Hebrew means "who works for himself". The Greek read it that way.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); all Hebrew manuscripts; KJV
readings.en: and has a servant
readings.plain: who has a servant

readings.w: Septuagint, the Old Greek of Proverbs: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed in Swete's edition (checked)
readings.en: serving himself
readings.plain: who works for himself

why: The consonants 'bd lw can be read 'eved lo, "a servant to him" (the Masoretic vowels), or 'oved lo, "working for himself". Both fit: better a modest man who has one servant, or a modest man who does his own work, than a show-off with no bread. The Plain follows the Masoretic vowels.

a: but the righteous man gets out of trouble.
t: An added couplet in the Greek (12:13a)
p: The Greek adds a couplet after the verse about gentle looks and harsh meetings at the gates.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); all Hebrew manuscripts
readings.en: and a righteous one comes out of trouble
readings.plain: but the righteous man gets out of trouble.

readings.w: Septuagint, the Old Greek of Proverbs: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed in Swete's edition (checked); Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus agree
readings.orig: ἐκφεύγει δὲ ἐξ αὐτῶν δίκαιος. (13a) ὁ βλέπων λεῖα ἐλεηθήσεται, ὁ δὲ συναντῶν ἐν πύλαις ἐκθλίψει ψυχάς
readings.en: but the righteous escapes from them. (13a) One who looks gently will be shown mercy, but one who confronts people in the gates will crush souls
readings.plain: but the righteous man escapes them. / One whose look is gentle will be shown mercy, / but one who picks quarrels at the gates will crush people.

why: The couplet is found only in the Greek; it is close in thought to 10:10 and 12:18. The Plain follows the Hebrew.

a: is paid back to him.
p: The marginal reading says someone (God) repays; the written text says the deed returns by itself.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (AD 1008): the reading the Masoretes marked to be read aloud (Qere); most modern versions
readings.en: he will repay to him
readings.plain: is paid back to him.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex: the written consonants (Ketiv)
readings.en: it will return to him
readings.plain: comes back to him.

why: The written text has the deed come back on its own; the marginal reading, followed by the Plain and most versions, has someone pay it back, which most read as God. The difference is small but has been used in debates about whether Proverbs sees reward as built into deeds or given by God.

a: but the road the wicked take sends them wandering.
t: A longer verse in the Greek
p: The Greek has three lines: a thoughtful righteous man is his own friend, and evil pursues sinners.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); all Hebrew manuscripts
readings.en: and the way of the wicked leads them astray
readings.plain: but the road the wicked take sends them wandering.

readings.w: Septuagint, the Old Greek of Proverbs: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed in Swete's edition (checked); Alexandrinus adds a further line
readings.orig: ἐπιγνώμων δίκαιος ἑαυτοῦ φίλος ἔσται, ἁμαρτάνοντας δὲ καταδιώξεται κακά, ἡ δὲ ὁδὸς τῶν ἀσεβῶν πλανήσει αὐτούς
readings.en: A discerning righteous man will be his own friend, but evil will pursue sinners, and the way of the ungodly will lead them astray
readings.plain: A righteous man with good judgment will be his own friend, / but trouble will hunt down those who sin, / and the road of the wicked will lead them astray.

why: The Greek seems to read the hard first line differently and adds a middle line found also at 13:21. The Plain follows the Hebrew; the note on the first line gives the readings of the verb.

a: and where its path goes, death is not.
p: The Hebrew says the path holds "no death". The Greek and many scholars read "to death".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); all Hebrew manuscripts; KJV
readings.en: and the way of its path: no death
readings.plain: and where its path goes, death is not.

readings.w: Septuagint, the Old Greek of Proverbs: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed in Swete's edition (checked)
readings.en: but the ways of those who bear grudges lead to death
readings.plain: but the ways of those who hold grudges lead to death.

readings.w: Proposed reading (vowels changed to 'el-mavet, many commentators)
readings.en: but a (wrong) path leads to death
readings.plain: but another path leads to death.

why: Many scholars think the vowels of 'al should be 'el, "to", which gives the usual contrast of life and death, as the Greek has. But 'al-mavet is the reading of the Hebrew text, and some scholars defend it as a statement that the righteous path leads beyond death. See the note.

a: is hard as rock.
p: The Hebrew word usually means "lasting". The Greek has "in ruin".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); all Hebrew manuscripts; KJV
readings.en: enduring, hard
readings.plain: is hard as rock.

readings.w: Septuagint, the Old Greek of Proverbs: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed in Swete's edition (checked)
readings.en: in destruction
readings.plain: leads to ruin.

why: The Greek gives the expected contrast, and some versions follow it. The Hebrew 'eitan can mean hard and unchanging, which fits a road no one can travel easily. The Plain keeps the Hebrew. See the note.

a: A messenger who is wicked drops into trouble,
p: The Greek read "king" instead of "messenger". With other vowels the verb means "makes others fall".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); all Hebrew manuscripts; KJV
readings.en: a wicked messenger falls into trouble
readings.plain: A messenger who is wicked drops into trouble,

readings.w: Septuagint, the Old Greek of Proverbs: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed in Swete's edition (checked)
readings.en: a rash king will fall into evils
readings.plain: A reckless king drops into trouble,

readings.w: Proposed reading (vowels changed to yappil, some commentators)
readings.en: a wicked messenger makes (others) fall into trouble
readings.plain: A messenger who is wicked drops others into trouble,

why: Mal'akh, "messenger", and melekh, "king", have the same first three consonants, and the Greek read the second. The parallel with "envoy" supports "messenger". Some scholars read the verb as causative, since a bad messenger harms the one who sent him (compare 10:26; 25:13). The Plain keeps the Masoretic Text.

a: The one who walks with the wise grows wise,
p: The written text has commands: "Walk with the wise and become wise." The marginal reading has a statement.

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (AD 1008): the reading the Masoretes marked to be read aloud (Qere); most modern versions
readings.en: one who walks with the wise becomes wise
readings.plain: The one who walks with the wise grows wise,

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex: the written consonants (Ketiv)
readings.en: walk with the wise and become wise
readings.plain: Walk with the wise and become wise,

why: The written consonants give two commands; the Masoretes marked them to be read as a statement, which matches the second line. The meaning is the same. The Plain follows the marginal reading, as most versions do.

a: The wisest of women builds her house,
p: The Hebrew vowels read "the wisest of women"; re-pointed, the same letters read "Wisdom", as in 9:1.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); all Hebrew manuscripts; KJV
readings.en: the wise ones of women
readings.plain: The wisest of women builds her house,

readings.w: The same Hebrew consonants with different vowels (chokhmot), proposed by many scholars, usually with "of women" taken as a gloss
readings.en: Wisdom
readings.plain: Wisdom builds her house,

readings.w: Septuagint, the Old Greek of Proverbs: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed in Swete's edition (checked)
readings.en: wise women built houses
readings.plain: Wise women build houses,

why: The Masoretic vowels, the same form as Judges 5:29, make the verse a saying about a woman who runs her household well, and the Greek also has wise women. Reading chokhmot ties the verse to Wisdom's house in 9:1 and to Woman Folly in 9:13–18, but it changes the vowels and usually drops a word. The Plain follows the Hebrew as pointed.

a: and the schemer is hated.
p: The Greek has "but a sensible man bears much", a contrast with the hothead.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); all Hebrew manuscripts; KJV
readings.en: and a man of schemes is hated
readings.plain: and the schemer is hated.

readings.w: Septuagint, the Old Greek of Proverbs: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed in Swete's edition (checked)
readings.en: but a sensible man puts up with much
readings.plain: but a sensible man puts up with much.

why: The Greek may have read yissa', "bears", for yissane', "is hated", and taken mezimmot in its good sense, "discretion". The Hebrew makes both lines about bad tempers: the hothead acts foolishly, the cold schemer is hated. The Plain keeps the Hebrew.

a: the lowly
p: The written text has 'aniyyim, "the poor"; the marginal reading has 'anawim, "the humble, lowly".

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (AD 1008): the reading the Masoretes marked to be read aloud (Qere); most modern versions
readings.en: humble, lowly
readings.plain: the lowly

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex: the written consonants (Ketiv)
readings.en: poor
readings.plain: the poor

why: The two words are close in form and meaning, and the Bible's scribes often wrote one for the other. "Lowly" covers both the poor and the humble. The Greek has "the poor" (ptōchous).

a: Their riches are the crown of the wise;
p: The Greek has "the shrewd man is the crown of the wise", as if the Hebrew read "their shrewdness".

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); all Hebrew manuscripts; KJV
readings.en: the crown of the wise is their wealth
readings.plain: Their riches are the crown of the wise;

readings.w: Septuagint, the Old Greek of Proverbs: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed in Swete's edition (checked)
readings.en: the crown of the wise is a shrewd man
readings.plain: Their shrewdness is the crown of the wise;

why: 'Ashram, "their wealth", and 'ormatam, "their shrewdness", look alike in Hebrew script. Some scholars prefer the Greek, which gives a smoother line about virtue. The Hebrew fits the book's view that wisdom often brings wealth (3:16; 8:18). The Plain keeps the Hebrew.

a: takes refuge in his death.
t: In his death, or in his integrity?
p: The Hebrew has "in his death". The Greek read "in his integrity", with two letters switched.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); all Hebrew manuscripts; KJV
readings.en: and the righteous takes refuge in his death
readings.plain: takes refuge in his death.

readings.w: Septuagint, the Old Greek of Proverbs: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed in Swete's edition (checked)
readings.orig: ὁ δὲ πεποιθὼς τῇ ἑαυτοῦ ὁσιότητι δίκαιος
readings.en: but the one who trusts in his own holiness is righteous
readings.plain: takes refuge in his integrity.

why: Hebrew bmwtw, "in his death", and btmw, "in his integrity", differ by two letters in a different order. Many scholars follow the Greek, since Proverbs rarely speaks of hope in death. The Plain keeps the Hebrew, which all Hebrew manuscripts have. See the note.

a: among fools, too, she makes herself known.
p: The Greek adds "not": wisdom is not recognized in the heart of fools.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); all Hebrew manuscripts; KJV
readings.en: and in the inner part of fools it is made known
readings.plain: among fools, too, she makes herself known.

readings.w: Septuagint, the Old Greek of Proverbs: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed in Swete's edition (checked)
readings.orig: ἐν δὲ καρδίᾳ ἀφρόνων οὐ διαγινώσκεται
readings.en: but in the heart of fools it is not recognized
readings.plain: but in the heart of fools she is not recognized.

why: The Greek gives the expected contrast, and several modern versions add "not". The Hebrew may be ironic (fools show off what little they know, compare 12:23) or may mean that wisdom makes itself known even among fools. The Plain keeps the Hebrew.

a: the mouth of fools
p: The written text has "the face of fools"; the marginal reading has "the mouth of fools".

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex (AD 1008): the reading the Masoretes marked to be read aloud (Qere); most modern versions
readings.en: and the mouth of fools
readings.plain: the mouth of fools

readings.w: Masoretic Text, Leningrad Codex: the written consonants (Ketiv)
readings.en: and the face of fools
readings.plain: the face of fools

why: The two words differ by one letter. "Mouth" fits the verb "grazes" and matches 15:2. The Plain follows the marginal reading, as most versions do.

a: and before honor goes humility.
t: Wisdom and glory in the Greek
p: The Greek reads "instruction and wisdom", and in place of humility before honor has glory answering to it.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); all Hebrew manuscripts
readings.en: and before honor, humility
readings.plain: and before honor goes humility.

readings.w: Septuagint, the Old Greek of Proverbs: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s AD) as printed in Swete's edition (checked)
readings.orig: φόβος θεοῦ παιδεία καὶ σοφία, καὶ ἀρχὴ δόξης ἀποκριθήσεται αὐτῇ
readings.en: The fear of God is instruction and wisdom, and the beginning of glory will answer to it
readings.plain: The fear of God is instruction and wisdom, / and the first of glory will answer to it.

why: The Greek has "God" for the LORD, joins instruction and wisdom, and lacks humility in the second line; a corrector of Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus add a line saying that glory comes to the humble. The Hebrew line returns at 18:12, and the Plain follows the Hebrew.
